Chateau Laurier,
Ottawa, November 29, 1915.
The Right Honourable
Sir Robert L. Borden, G.C.M.G., etc.,
*	Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-I think it may be convenient if I place on record a brief narrative of the circumstances since my arrival in Canada leading up to the changes which are now to be made in the constitution of the purchasing agency for munitions of war in Canada on behalf of the British Government. These changes, which are the logical consequence of the altered conditions, have been approved by H. R. H. the Governor General and your Government, and I am therefore authorized by the Minister of Munitions to announce that they will come into force as from November 30, 1915.
Since my arrival in Canada on October 26, as representative in this country of the Minister of Munitions in succession to Mr. D. A. Thomas, my colleague Mr. R. H. Brand and myself have, * at the request of yourself and General Sir Sam Hughes, concentrated our attention upon this problem of adaptation to the changed conditions. That a re-organization was necessary to meet the altered circumstances was generally recognized by all those most intimately connected with the Shell Committee, and General Bertram was among the first to call our attention to the fact, and to suggest that the new problems of administration on a greatly increased scale required for their proper direction an expanded organization
The Shell Committee, which was appointed in September, 1914, by the Minister of Militia and Defence, to deal with the munitions orders placed in Canada by the Imperial Government has, I think, met with remarkable success in dealing with a difficult task.
It is an astonishing thing that the work of the Shell Committee was so satisfactory to both these representatives of the British Government, and yet is so unsatisfactory to my right hon, friend, who probably does not know a hundredth part of what these two men knew who personally investigated
the whole matter for several weeks. If we are to place these two opinions before the people of Capada, I wonder which they will choose: that of the men who investigated the work of the Shell Committee from day to day for weeks and even months, or the opinion of my right hon. friend, who rises in this House and bases, his aspersions on the Shell Committee upon nothing higher or stronger than newspaper rumours. (Continuing to read):
In the early days the problem was to persuade manufacturers to undertake the work of making shells, which was quite new to them, and presented formidable difficulties that caused many of the leading firms to hold back The orders at that time destined for this country were on a small scale; there was naturally no assurance of continuity in the work, and the prospects of success were doubtful. The readiness with which Canadian manufacturers adapted themselves to a new industry is, I think, remarkable, and although as in England, they have often been unable to live up to their original promises, yet they have nothing to fear from a comparison of the early efforts of firms of the highest standing.
Speaking generally, I think it may be said that the earlier difficulties have now been overcome, and the work of the administering body in Canada has entered upon a new phase. In the first place, it has been realized that shells can be successfully and profitably manufactured in Canada, and, instead of holding back, there is now a keen competition on the part of manufacturers to secure contracts. Secondly, the volume of orders placed in Canada has grown at. a very rapid rate, and the output both of shell cases and component parts has increased so largely as to require a -more highly organized department to ensure efficient co-ordination and prompt deliveries. Thus, from a small beginning, the activities of the Shell Committee have grown with startling rapidity and now embrace the administration of funds more than twice as large as the annual revenues of the Dominion Government. It is obvious, therefore, that the original organization needs amendment to conform to the actualities of to-day.
I should like to take this opportunity to point out, after a careful inquiry into the facts, that the Shell Committee has been subjected to much unfair criticism. It was, as I have said, appointed to deal with the orders of modest proportions, and from the nature of the case was intended to be educative rather than administrative. It was natural, therefore, that it should contain an infusion of steel manufacturers, whose advice and experience were necessary to the proper development of the new industry. The measure of their success can be gauged by the remarkable results achieved. The facts speak for themselves. There are now some 320 firms in Canada manufacturing shells or their component parts, and in the short space of fourteen months the Shell Committee, with the active encouragement and support of General Sir Sam Hughes, have developed the largest industry in the whole of the Dominion. They have been the means also of bringing into being certain important industries subsidiary to shell making which will have a permanent effect in developing the resources of the country. For example: copper has hitherto been produced in the form of " matte " and sent to the United States for refining. Arrangements have now been made

for the refining to be undertaken in Canada, and a new plant will shortly be in operation which will give an impetus to the copper mining industry of the country. Similarly, Canadian zinc ores which contain about equal quantities of lead and zinc, have hitherto been shipped from Canada in the raw state. Owing to the demand created by the war orders and the encouragement of the Shell Committee, the electric refining of zinc is now being developed in Canada on a commercial scale, and this, together with the derivative industries connected therewith, will, there is good reason to believe, now be established on a permanent basis in Canada. Brass will also shortly be made in the country on a considerable scale. A great impetus has likewise been given to the manufacture of explosives: nitro-cellulose powder, tri-nitrotoluol and sabulite are now being produced on a large scale and at moderate prices. Canadian competition has resulted in keeping down the price of these commodities, and has enabled the Shell Committee to effect large economies. Important fields of industry have thus been opened up in Canada as a result of the activities of the Shell Committee. It would be outside the scope of this letter to suggest that the time has come when attention should be paid to the question how these new industries and those derivative from them, which owe their origin to the great demand for munitions of war, can best be developed and encouraged so as to form a permanent part of the industrial fabric of Canada, but no doubt your Government is fully alive to the situation. As a result of the war industries set in motion under the auspices of General Sir Sam Hughes and the Shell Committee, an army of some 100,000 skilled mechanics and workmen has been maintained and trained up in Canada. They are a permanent asset to the country, and the skill which they have acquired will be of lasting benefit after the war in building up the commercial prosperity of Canada.
These far-reaching and important results have not been achieved without the most exacting and strenuous labour, which has fallen more particularly upon General Bertram and Colonel Carnegie, and which a single-minded enthusiasm for the cause has enable them to sustain. Perhaps I may be allowed to add also that these striking results owe their inception and a large measure of their development to the practical zeal and the active encouragement of General Sir Sam Hughes. To conceive a big idea is hard, but to give effect to it in action demands qualities of a rarer kind. I wish therefore to place on record that the Shell Committee have for the past fourteen months been carrying on a work of the most exacting and strenuous nature, and that they have fulfilled their task well. Tiie changes, therefore, which are now being made are the logical development of their work-the necessary superstructure upon the foundations laid by them.	1
As explained to me by yourself and General Sir Sam Hughes, it Is the wish of your Government that, since in actual practice all munitions orders for the Imperial Government are placed by the British Ministry of Munitions with the Shell Committee, there should be a direct relation between the purchasing agency and that department which, since the establishment of the Shell Committee, has been constituted to deal with munition supplies, and that this logical business connection should be given effect to now that the extended scope of the functions of the committee make a re-organization imperative. ' In order to carry out your wishes and to make it clear that the purchasing agency is administratively independent of 
the Canadian Government, the members of the existing ^ shell Committee have tendered their resignations to the Minister of Militia, by whom they were appointed, and a new board entitled the " Imperial Munitions Board " has been constituted by the British Minister of Munitions as from November 30, 1915, to deal with such purchases of munitions supplies as may from time to time be entrusted to it by the said minister. All the rights and powers heretofore vested in the Shell Committee, together with all the moneys at the committe's credit, have been transferred to and vested in the "Imperial Munitions Board," and the Shell Committee has been relieved from all liabilities, which will be assumed by the new board acting on behalf of the Minister of Munitions.
The " Imperial Munitions Board " has therefore been appointed by and is responsib e to the British Minister of Munitions. At the same time, however, it is clearly of vital importance that the support and co-operation of the Canadian Government should be maintained, and that there should be some " nexus " between the Imperial Government, the Canadian Government and the purchasing agency. The Minister of Militia will in any case, I know, use all his influence to support the development of munitions supplies in Canada. But it is very valuable that there should be a recognized continuity in the work, and that it should be clearly seen that the new hoard will receive from him the same encouragement and support that has contributed so materially to the success of the Shell Committee. At the request, therefore, of the Minister of Munitions, General the Honourable Sir Sam Hughes, K.C.B., Minister of Militia and Defence, has accepted the position of Honorary President of the Imperial Munitions Board.
The following gentlemen, with their consent, have been appointed members of the board :
J. W. Flavelle, Esq., (Chairman with executive and administrative powers).
Gen. Alex. Bertram, (Deputy Chairman).
Hon. Colonel David Carnegie.
G. H. Dawson, Esq.
C. B. Gordon. Esa.
J. A. Vaillancourt, Esq.
E. R. Wood, Esq.
Mr. J. W. Flavelle has with great public spirit undertaken to make the work of the board his primary consideration, and he has made the necessary arrangements to this end.
I am glad also to be able to tell you that Mr. C. B. Gordon, of Montreal, has kindly promised to devote a great part of his time to the work, and I am confident that his wide business experience and reputation will contribute largely to the success of the undertaking.
I take this opportunity of giving public recognition on behalf of the Minister of Munitions to the valuable services rendered by the members of the Shell Committee in developing the resources of Canada for the production of munitions of war. They have been willing to lend their services during the period of development, when their experience, which has been freely given, has been of the greatest assistance in overcoming the initial difficulties. But these have now been surmounted, and the justification no longer exists for a board of experts. At the same time it would be a great loss if the wide experience they have acquired were not made available to the new " Imperial Munitions Board," and I attach great value to the assurance they have generously given that they

will be willing to afford every assistance in their power to the new board.
I have the honour to be. sir,
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. L. Hichens.
A good deal has been said about the high prices paid for shells in Canada, and hon. gentlemen in this House and journals in the country have spoken of the exactions of Canadian manufacturers from the British Government through the Shell Committee.

We never put it that way; it was the folly of the Shell 'Committee we spoke of.
Sir ROiBERIT BORDEN: My hon. friend is not the only hon. member of this House. He need not take upon himself such a character of universality as he is attributing to himself at this moment. I did not make any particular allusion to him, but was speaking quite generally. I put to Mir. Hichens the same inquiry as to his appreciation of the gentlemen who constitute the Shell Committee as. that which I had put to Mr. Thomas, and I received from him precisely title same answer as to the integrity, honour, and good faith of all the members of that committee. He stated in the most unqualified terms that with regard to them he had not one word to say beyond this, that he believed them to be men of the highest honour and of perfect integrity, men who had, to the utmost of their ability, discharged what appeared to them to be a patriotic duty.
After endeavouring to get some comparisons of the prices paid for shells in Canada and elsewhere, I wrote to Mr. Hichens on the subject. Although my right hon. friend, has not said very much about this phase of the question, it is my duty to say a few words in regard to it, on account of what has been said here and elsewhere. Pn the 6th of December, 1915, I wrote to Mr. Hichens this letter:
Dear Mr. Hichens,-I enclose a copy of a letter I have received from the Minister of Finance. Is it possible to get some authoritative statement as to the comparative prices being paid for machining and forging shells in England, Canada and the United States?
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) R. L. Borden.
This is Sir Thomas White's letter addressed to myself:
Ottawa, December 4, 1915.
Dear Sir Robert,-I have a letter this morning from the President of the Dominion Steel Foundry Company, of Hamilton, who states,
among other things, that prices paid in England for machining and forging are from tep to fifty per cent greater than in Canada and that the present prices here average lower than prices being paid in United States. He states further that the cost of labour and of raw material is increasing daily, while the price of shells is going down. I think it advisable as soon as you have authentic information on the subject that a statement should be given to the press as to the comparative prices being paid for machining and forging shells, in England, Canada and United, States. Such a statement would go a long way towards meeting adverse criticism of certain of the press and in vindicating the work of the Shell Committee.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. T. White.
Mr. Hichens replied to my letter on the 8th day of December as follows:
Dear Sir Robert,-With reference to your letter of December 6th, I regret that I have not got the necessary figures for the purpose of making a comparison between English, Canadian and American prices for shells. I suggest that you write to Mr. Lloyd George asking him to give you a full report in regard to these comparative prices, since there has been a certain amount of criticism of the prices paid in Canada, and since you are anxious to know the real facts of the position. It would be better, I think, that this should come officially from the Ministry of Munitions at home, and I think that, speaking generally, they will be able to satisfy you that Canadian prices have not been unreasonable.
I have seen it suggested in the press that there should be a full inquiry into the doings of the Shell Committee, and I hope it will not be found necessary to give way to this demand. Personally, I am entirely satisfied that the Shell Committee have carried out their work well, and I feel that such inquiry would merely hamper the work of the new Munitions Board. They have a great deal to do, and I should be sorry if their activities were interfered with in this way. There is also perhaps something in the point that the Shell Committee was acting for the Imperial Government, and that any enquiry should be made rather on their instruction or at their request, than by the authority of the Canadian Government.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) W. D. Hichens.
As my ihon. friend smiles at that, I may say that that letter was written to me without any suggestion as to the concluding paragraph, whigh I had never discussed with Mr. Hichens.
What I was smiling at was rather that Ihe should presume to advise the Prime Minister as to the desirability of holding an investigation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I suppose Mr. Hichens, being responsible for the establishment of the Imperial Munitions Board, was desirous, as he expressed it, that its work should not be hampered, and a little later on in the course of my remarks I

shall give in regard to that some information which will, perhaps, commend itself to my right hon. friend.
I sent the letter of the Minister of Finance to Sir George Perley, who mac^e application to the Minister of Munitions, and, as the reply which we received was marked "confidential and secret," we asked for liberty to publish it, and the letteT which we received thereupon from Sir Herbert Llewellyn Smith, Secretary of the Ministry of Munitions, is as follows: January 20, 1916.
Sir,-In reply to your letter of the 13 th January on the subject of prices paid for shells, I am directed by the Minister of Munitions to inform you that it is the general rule not to give publicity to contract prices, and that consequently Mr. Lloyd George would prefer that the letter referred to should not be published.
I am, however, to add that there would be no objection to Sir Robert Borden making use of any part of the information so furnished, if in his discretion he should think such a course desirable.
I am, etc.,
(Sgd.) H. Llewellyn Smith.
I have made some extracts from the portions of that confidential letter which do not set forth prices. I am ready to read them to the House; I am also perfectly ready to give to the House, not the prices, but an exact comparison between the prices paid in Great Britain and in the United States and those paid in Canada; doing that, not by stating the actual prices paid, but by fixing the British price at the figure 1 and the Canadian and American prices at corresponding figures.

The Minister of Militia and Defence, speaking in this House on the 26th of January, gave prices of many kinds of shells and parts thereof as of the 8th day of December last. Will the Prime Minister say whether or not those prices, which will be found on page 301 of Hansard, are the same as those contained in his memorandum?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am not going 'to say anything about that, because I re'ally have not compared them; but those portions of the letter which do not contain actual prices I am perfectly willing to read to the House, and I am also willing to give comparative prices paid for shells in England, Canada, and the United States. This memorandum gives a general comparison of the prices first when they were high everywhere and then at a considerably later date when they were lower. It is known here, as everywhere else, that the

prices paid for shells are very much less now in all three countries than they were at first.

When I addressed the
House on a former occasion I dealt to some extent with the question of prices, and I will do so again, but I do not think that my right hon. friend can properly quote from a letter without laying it on the table. My right hon. friend purposes, not to give the prices, but to make a sort of algebraic comparison.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In that case I
will not read the letter; but I can at least do this: I can state that I have the best of information, that of the British Ministry of Munitions, that prices in Great Britain were very much higher in the first instance than they were afterwards. It is equally true that prices in Great Britain varied as between different firms and according to conditions on which different contracts were made.
The production of some of these shells was familiar to certain manufacturers in Great Britain, 'but unfamiliar to others, and the prices accorded to the manufacturers who were not previously familiar with t'he business of shell-making, were considerably higher than the prices accorded to those who had previous experience, and who, therefore, could make the shells at a smaller cost. I would like, also, to point out that manufacturers in Canada, besides having to equip themselves with plant, had to become familiar with the process of manufacturing. Generally speaking, the prices paid in Canada compare very favourably, indeed, with those paid in Great Britain and the United! States, according to the authoritative information which has been placed in my hands by the British Ministry of Munitions. I believe that the prices paid for shrapnel shells in the first instance were a little higher in Canada than those paid in Great Britain to firms who had no previous experience, but they were a little lower than the prices paid in the United States to firms having no previous experience. I have the same authority for my statement when I say, so far as the 18-pounder high explosive shell is concerned, which was taken up by the Canadian Shell Committee after they and the Canadian manufacturers had had some experience with the shrapnel shell, that the prices paid in Canada compared most favourably with the prices paid in Great Britain and

in tlhe United States. Further, the Canadian Shell Committee, in one of the latest contracts which it made, as I am informed on the same unimpeachable authority, succeeded in getting the 4 -5-inch high explosive shell, together with the cartridge case and primer, for about the same price that is being paid in the United Kingdom for the shell alone. That result is, of course, regarded as most satisfactory by the Imperial authorities. I say further, that if we take either the highest price paid in Canada or the lowest price paid in Canada for the shells of larger sizes-that i's to say, the 6-inch high explosive shell, the 8-inch shell, and the 9-2-inch shell-the highest price paid in Canada is lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and is lower than the highest price paid in the United, States in one instance, and very little higher in two other instances.
Is it not true that one of the objections raised by Mr. Thomas was that the Canadian prices were too high?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Thomas said they were too high. And Mr. Lloyd George has shown, in his address in the House of Commons, that the price of the 18-pounder shrapnel had been reduced 40 per cent in price in Great Britain and the 'howitzer shells 30 per cent. He said, also, that very high prices were paid in Great Britain in the first instance. I venture to say that if an investigation were ordered it would be found that for the 18-pounder high explosive shell, the highest price paid in Canada was 11 per cent lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and very much lower than the highest price paid in the United States. It will be found further that for the 4-5-inch shell the highest price paid in Canada was 17 per cent lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and 15 per cent lower than the highest price paid in the United States. One contract given in the United States was very much higher, but I exclude it as it was a single order and given for special delivery. For the 6-inch high explosive shell, the highest price paid in Canada was 17 per cent lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and 9 per cent lower than the highest price paid in the United States. For the 8-inch shell, the highest price paid in Canada was 26 per cent lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and 2 per cent higher than the highest price in the United States. For
the 9-2-inch shell, the highest price paid in Canada was 16 per cent lower than the highest price paid in Great Britain, and one per cent higher than the highest price paid in the United States.

I am informed on
reliable authority that the position taken by Mr. Thomas was that Canadian prices were higher than those in the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am giving to the House information on my own responsibility as a member of the House and as a minister of the Crown-information which comes to me as authentic and which I believe to be absolutely correct.

I desire to ask a question for information; I am perfectly honest about this. Can the Prime Minister tell us when the first order was given in Canada for the 6-inch shell, the 8-inch shell, and 9 -2 inch high explosive shell?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I really do not know. I think it was about six months ago.

Can the right hon.
gentleman get that information?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes, if it will add to the happiness of my hon. friend, I will try to get that information for him.
The time of the giving of orders would be important.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The time of any order, of course, is important. I could go on and give figures for the lowest prices paid. For the 4.5 inch high-explosive shell, the lowest price paid in Canada was 22 per cent lower than the lowest price paid in Great Britain, while the lowest price paid in the United States was 2 per cent higher than that paid in Great Britain. For the 6-inch high-explosive shell, the lowest price paid in Canada was 4 per cent lower than the lowest price paid in Great Britain, and the same as the lowest in the United States. For the 8-inch shell, the lowest price paid in Canada was 6 per cent lower than the lowest price paid in Great Britain, while the lowest price paid in the United States was 14 per cent lower than that paid in Great Britain. For the 9.2-inch shell, the lowest price paid in Canada was 6 per cent lower than the lowest price paid in Great Britain while the lowest price paid in United States was 17 per cent lower than that paid in Great Britain.

Now, considering the industrial development of Canada, considering the absolute inexperience of our manufacturers in the production of munitions of war, I venture to say that under the organization of the Shell Committee, those manufacturers deserve every possible praise for what they have accomplished, and that the aspersions cast upon them, whether by my right hon. friend or the press of this country, are absolutely undeserved in view of the results that have been attained.. *
At six o'clock the House took recess. *
The House resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.

Bill No. 50, for the relief of Raymond Conliffe Savage.-Mr. Douglas.
Bill No. 51, for the relief of Harry Lome White Cunningham.-Mr. T. J. Stewart.
Consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for the appointment of a special committee to inquire into purchase of shells, etc., resumed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had been dealing with comparative prices in Great Britain, the United States, and Canada. Not much more remains to be said on this subject. To sum up, our prices at first for 18-pound shrapnel, with which we began in Canada, were slightly higher than the prices in Great Britain and slightly lower than those in the United States. The reason for this is perfectly simple. We had then no experience in the manufacture of shells in Canada, and there were no continuation orders allowed for. At that time it was not believed in Great Britain, here of elsewhere that the war would last so long as it has unfortunately lasted, and so continuation orders were not given. There was no assurance that there would be further orders, and the manufacturers who undertook this work and who had to equip plants with machinery for the purpose necessarily had to demand higher prices than they would have demanded if they had been assured of orders extending over a year or 18 months. Upon information given to me from the highest authoritative quarter I assert that in respect of all other shells produced in Canada such as 18-pound high explosives, 4.5's and all other 
large shells, the production of which we began last summer, the prices in Canada
have been, on the whole, lower than in either of the other two countries I have mentioned. In 90 per cent of the cases the prices in Canada have been at least as low as those paid by the British Government in any other part of the world. I also affirm, from equally authoritative information, that while here, as in Great Britain, the deliveries have not been up to what was anticipated, nevertheless they are at the present time very good indeed, and I am confident they will compare favourably with those made in the United States. I have the warrant of a very high authority, a representative of the British Government in the United States at the present time, for the assertion which I am now making. So, before we begin to belittle our own country in that regard, I think it would be just as well for us to consider what has been done by other countries. My right hon. friend forgets that Mr. Lloyd George, in his speech delivered in the British House of Commons on the 20th day of December , last, stated that last spring, when he undertook his duties as Minister of Munitions, deliveries in Great Britain were only 16 per cent of what they ought to be, and that under the Ministry of Munitions between that date and the 20th of December last deliveries had increased from 16 per cent to 80 per cent. They had not reached the high-water mark of anticipation even during the period from March, when he took charge, until December, when he made his speech. There are one or two quotations which I should like to read from that speech. In speaking of prices, Mr. Lloyd George said:
The prices were fixed for gun ammunition when the need was very urgent. There was no time to bargain, and that is true both of the War Office and of the Ministry of Munitions. New firms were also taken on, but at first the actual cost of production of unaccustomed and inexperienced firms is very considerably higher than that of experienced firms, so that for one reason or another prices were high.
Then, speaking of the effort made by the Ministry of Munitions to reduce prices, he said:	,
Therefore it has not yet come to full fruition, but I will just give the House an indication of the saving which will be effected by this means. The cost of the ammunition for 18-pounders, which is a very considerable item, running into millions, has been reduced by 40 per cent, and the cost of ammunition for 4.5 howitzers has been reduced by 30 per cent, since the report of this Committee, and all the new contracts are based on these prices.

Further on he said:
Contracts are being placed very largely through these local munitions committees. At first it was always necessary to let contracts at fairly high prices, because there were unaccustomed firms coming in, and they would not make much out of it, although the prices were high.
The condition which Mr. Lloyd George here sets out as prevailing in Great Britain at that time prevailed to a more intense degree in Canada, where we had had absolutely no experience in the production of ammunition, except a slight experience in the Dominion Arsenal at Quebec, and it ill becomes any citizen of this country to make an attack on the efforts that have been made in Canada during the past 18 months. I think the efforts have had a splendid success, one of which Canadians on the whole have every reason to be proud. I do not pretend for one moment that the Shell Committee did not make mistakes. I do not believe that any of its members would pretend that that committee did not make mistakes. To say otherwise would be to declare that they were infallible, and they know that they are fallible, as all the rest of us are; but I do say that the enlisting of the manufacturers of Canada, reluctantly at first, to undertake these great operations, and the splendid and conspicuous success which it has proved to be in the past 18 months, deserves commendation and not the condemnation of any man in this House. I have under my hand and could read the record of what one company did in about four and a half months in Canada, since some very large orders were placed with it in October or November last. The record would surprise this House. You would hardly believe that it could have been accomplished i,n Canada; and yet my right hon. friend says that the object of his motion is to probe and remddy conditions. Does he propose to attack the Imperial Munitions Board? I venture to think that that board is doing splendid service for Canada, as the Shell Committee did. How is he going to probe and remedy conditions in respect to the Shell Committee, since that committee is functus officio, and has handed over its duties to the Imperial Munitions Board, upon which some of the members of the Shell Committee still sit? Probe and remedy conditions, he says. I venture to say that if I handed in this statement of what one company has accomplished my right hon. friend would not say, nor would anyone else, that any board
could improve on the record which it contains. It is a remarkable and splendid record; and so I say that, on the yrhole, my right hon. friend has not made any case 'for investigation, except on hearsay information which he has derived from newspapers, and upon which, indeed, he does not base any charge on his own behalf.
So far as the Imperial Munitions Board is concerned, the Government of Canada proposes to co-operate with that board precisely as it co-operated with the Shell Committee. If the Imperial Munitions Board comes to the Government of Canada, and desires us to assist them or to co-operate with them, or makes any representation to us, the object of which is to increase production of munitions in Canada, or to give greater opportunities to develop the resources of this country, we shall co-operate with the Imperial Munitions Board precisely as we co-operated with the Shell Committee. In doing that, I am sure we shall be adopting a course to which my right hon. friend, or any other member of the House, can take no exception.
My right -hon. friend speaks of the Shell Committee having handed out contracts to middlemen without any effort at all to ascertain whether or not the persons to whom the contracts were handed were in a position to fulfil them. In other words, I suppose my right hon. friend is bringing a charge either of favoritism or of negligence or of political influence against the Shell Committee; his statements in that regard were so vague that I really do not know what it was he intended precisely to suggest. He spoke of a patronage list. If he desires to suggest or insinuate that there was any patronage list in a political sense, or that the members of this Government interfered with the placing of those orders, then I am in a position to give a most emphatic contradiction to my right hon. friend. Never, from first to last, was there the slightest attempt to exercise political influence over the Shell Committee; on the contrary, I have had repeated complaints from political friends throughout the country that gentlemen of the opposite political faith were going to the Shell Committee and procuring contracts for their constituents and friends, which Conservative members of Parliament and other Conservatives throughout the country could not procure. There are gentlemen on

the other side of the House within the sound of my voice who know that I am speaking the truth in that regard, and last but not least among them is my right hon. friend himself. If I am not mistaken, he went to the Shell Committee with a friend or constituent and succeeded in securing a fairly good order for him.
I deny that absolutely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Did my right hon. friend not visit the Shell Committee with a friend?

Yes I went *with a friend, a constituent from Victoria-ville, in the county of Arthabaska. I was received by General Bertram, to whom I introduced tlie gentleman. I said to General Bertram: " I ho-pe there is no favouritism; I have simply come here to introduce this gentleman, and to tell you that he is quite capable to fulfil his contract."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not suppose that any other member of Parliament, if other members of Parliament went to the Shell Committee, did anything else. I can say to my right hon. friend that, if all reports are true, he was very much more successful with the Shell Committee than some Conservative members of Parliament, because I understand-I speak subject to correction-that the gentleman who accompanied my right hon. friend on his visit to the Shell Committee did succeed in getting a very substantial order .
That is not what he told me. He told me that the order was not very substantial. As to what he wanted, I do not know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It might not
have heen as large as my right hon. friend and his constituent desired, but his efforts were very much more successful than those of a good many Conservative members who went to the Shell Committee and got nothing. My right hon. friend did get something, and it strikes me that, having been so courteously received, and having been so successful on behalf of his friend and constituent, it is, to say the least, a case of black ingratitude that he should cast the reflections upon the Shell Committee which we heard this afternoon. After I had returned from Great Britain, I saw, or at least I heard, that there had been paraded in the Liberal press throughout the

country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, an alleged charge by Mr. D. A. Thomas, now Lord Rhondda, that the Government of Canada were using political influence in connection with the Shell Committee. That statement was published in the Montreal Herald, over which my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) presides, and it was published I think in every Liberal newspaper from one end of the country to the other.
Mr. 'GRAHAM: Was that an interview with Mr. Thomas, or a speech by him?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: My right hon. friend referred to the Peterborough Review as having published one editorial article, and in reading the next page he referred to the Peterborough Examiner. Which one was it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Peterborough Examiner is the name of the paper mentioned in the letters.

My right hon. friend in
reading one letter quoted the Peterborough Review as wanting an inquiry and in the next breath it was the Peterborough Examiner. Which is it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is the Peterborough Examiner.
Now I come to a question which my right hon. friend dealt with in his endeavour to make it appear that it is an entirely proper thing for the Government to Refuse to bring down papers in respect to matters transacted by a department of the Government for the United Kingdom, whereas it is a highly improper thing to take the same course and to refuse an inquiry in respect to matters transacted by a committee acting directly for the British Government and under its direction. That is the point which my right hon. friend makes. Let us see just what his position was in 1903. The question came up then as to whether or not certain papers should be brought down in
respect, to business carried on and orders fulfilled by a department of the Government, of which he was the head, for the British Government. My hon. friend says that there is a great difference between this case and that case because that was a motion foT inquiry and this is a motion for cause. It seems to be a remarkable position, that, in respect to a matter as to which the papers cannot be brought down, nevertheless an inquiry can be had. That strikes one as a remarkable distinction. If the subject is a proper one for inquiry in this Parliament, one would suppose that it would be a proper thing to have the papers brought down in order that an inquiry might be founded upon them; at least, that appeals to my sense of what is logical and reasonable, although, apparently, it does not so appeal to my right hon. friend. What was the position which my right hon. friend took in 1903? He took this position, first, through his Finance Minister, who spoke for him in that regard, and next through his own lips. Mr. Fielding said:
For all expenditure of the public money of Canada, the ministers are accountable to this House and the House is entitled to every information, but this is an expenditure of Imperial money for which this Government is not accountable to this House.
Further on:
If this were the public money of the Dominion, my hon. friend's motion would be a proper one, and we would he bound to bring down a return showing how it was expended.
Further on:
The matter would he a proper one to he brought forward in the Parliament of Great Britain but not in this House.
Why? For the reason that the money was the money of the United Kingdom for which the ministers were accountable to the Parliament of the United Kingdom and this Parliament had therefore no right to inquire into its expenditure. Further on:
As the money expended was not that of the people of Canada, there is no ground on which this Government can be called to an account here for that expenditure.
And my right hon. friend himself said:
We have had no complaint from the British Government, and I therefore see no reason why this House should inquire into the expenditure of money which does not concern it.
Not only in this case have we had no complaint from the British Government, but we have had express statements from representatives of the British Government in this country that they are entirely satisfied with the work which the Shell Committee has done on their behalf.

There is another matter which I woulfl like to bring to the attention of the House and the attention of my right hon. friend: It was not during the Boer war, nor has it been during this war, the practice of the British Government to favour or to grant inquiries into such matters during the progress of the war. The subject came up during the Boer war. An inquiry was moved for in the British House of Commons. The question which arose and which had to be determined by the leaders on that occasion was not as to whether an inquiry should be held, because all agreed that an inquiry must be held, but as to whether or not that inquiry should be interjected into the middle of the war, or whether it should form part of a general inquiry into the conduct of the war to take place at its conclusion. This is what Mr. Balfour said on that subject:
Then comes the question of the date of the inquiry. It had better begin as soon as the war, to use the phrase of my right honourable. friend, is substantially over, and as soon as the necessary witnesses are obtainable. I hope that statement is sufficiently extensive and explicit.
Mr. Asquith, speaking in the same debate, said:
The Government promise that they will form part of the general inquiry which is to take place at the close of the war, and that the facts so far as they are ascertained, will thus be brought to the light of day. On that distinct assurance I think my honourable friend may be well content with the result he has achieved in initiating the debate and that he should not in accordance with the general feelings of the House proceed to a division.
So the motion for an inquiry was withdrawn not only at the request of Mr. Balfour, the leader of the Government, but at the request of Mr. Asquith, the leader of the Opposition. That had reference to a general inquiry in regard to matters in connection with the war. But later on the question was raised as to an inquiry more like that which my right hon. friend proposes here. A member asked whether an inquiry would be held into the hiring of transports, the prices paid, the length of the passages, tfie food supplied to the troops on the transports, and the question why the fast mail steamers subsidized by the Government were not requisitioned. Mr. Balfour answered that this would form part of the general inquiry to he held at the end of the war.
What date is that?

we shall reimburse the British Government for these necessary supplies to our troops at the front. In some cases, perhaps, the prices charged to us may be higher and in other cases lower than the prices which we pay in this country. Does my right hon. friend propose that we should stop in the midst of this war and conduct a Parliamentary inquiry into the cost of all these articles for the purpose of ascertaining whether the British Government is charging us too much or too little? Why, I venture to think that my right hon. friend would not for one moment make a suggestion of that kind, and yet that is the course to which his motion points, if there is really any reason at all behind his motion, and I must confess that in my opinion there is really nothing behind it.
Upon all these considerations I greatly regret that my right hon. friend has seen fit to make the motion, and accompany it with the speech he has made to-day. As far as an investigation into the work of the Shell Committee is concerned, that investigation has been made to the extent desired by the British Government, first by Mr. Thomas, and next by Mr. Hichens. They expressed themselves as perfectly satisfied with the course the Shell Committee had taken and with the work which it had done.
Now, what course does the Government propose to take with regard to the motion which my right hon. friend has proposed to this House? As far as the Shell Committee is concerned-I shall speak afterwards of another matter-our proposal is this:	We
shall direct the attention of the British Government in detail to every charge, allegation and rumour brought up in this House or elsewhere by my right hon. friend or by any of his supporters with regard to the Shell Committee. We shall further inform the British Government that if an inquiry is thought advisable, we are prepared to co-operate with them to the fullest extent, and to issue any commission, take any proceedings, pass any legislation, and do any other act for the purpose of making that inquiry as full, thorough, and complete as they deem advisable. But without their consent or approval, we da not propose to enter upon an investigation or inquire into such expenditures by the British Government, especially as such an inquiry could not fail to interfere very seriously with the work carried on by the Imperial Munitions Board, which at present conducts a business involving the payment of not less than $5,000,000 per week.
c.Sir Robert Borden. ]
Such is our position with regard to that. As a matter of fact, during the last session of Parliament, for six weeks the .staff of the Department of Militia and Defence were prevented from carrying on their ordinary duties, and the interest of this country suffered because they were employed in doing nothing but attending the Public Accounts Committee and looking up the papers demanded by hon. gentlemen opposite. The business of this country in connection with the war thus practically stopped for six weeks; and so far as I am concerned, I do not intend, without, the express approval and sanction of the British Government, to stop the business of the Imperial Munitions Board. My right hon. friend with one breath tells us that munitions, more munitions, and still more munitions, are required at the front; and with the next he proposes a resolution that, if passed, could not fail to prevent the production of munitions in this country upon as great a scale as would be both possible and desirable.
I have something else to say to my right hon. friend. On many occasions in the past he has laid down in very plain language the rule with regard to making charges. In 1897, when a certain allegation was made in the House, he said ,to the then leader of the Opposition, Sir Charles Tupper:
If he will make a charge plain and substantial that we can understand, I will meet him, but I will have no cowardly insinuations in regard to that matter.
-He said on another occasion, in 1897, in reply to the late Mr. Davin:
If the hon. gentleman wishes to make a charge against any member of the Government, or any member of this House, there is a proper way to do so, and conform to the rules of the House, viz: to make a personal statement on his responsibility as a member of the House, conclude his statement with a charge, and that charge must then be investigated.
And he has used similar language in this House on various other occasions. I have his declarations under my hand, but I do not intend to weary the House with them. If, however, he or any of his followers has a charge to make against any member of the Government with respect to the Shell Committee or with respect to anything else, let him or his follower stand up in his place, and on his responsibility as a member, make that charge, and it will be investigated thoroughly and completely. The

Shell Committee is one thing; the Government's responsibility in connection with it is another. I thoroughly admit what responsibility we had with regard to the Shell Committee, namely, to appoint men of good Tepute, of high character, of experience, of recognized ability, and to co-operate with them so far as in us lay in order that they might do their best to develop the industries of this country for the production of munitions. But there is something else to foe said, and I repeat that, if my right hon. friend, or any of his followers, has any charge to make against a member of the Government in regard to any of these matters-let him make that charge in distinct and understandable terms, and he will have the investigation as soon as he so desires.
I regret to have detained the House at such great length with regard to this subject, but it is an important one, and it has , been much misrepresented in the press of Canada, and I think in this House to a very considerable extent. I therefore thought it my duty as head of the Government to make absolutely clear to this House and to tihe people of Canada just what the connection of the Government was with the Shell Committee, and what it is with the Imperial Munitions Board, and to make it clear, also, that, as far as either the Shell Committee or the Imperial Munitions Board is concerned, we have absolutely nothing to conceal and nothing to fear. If any investigation is sanctioned or approved by the British Government in regard to either the Shell Committee or the Imperial Munitions Board, we have mot the slightest objection, and we will assist and co-operate in every way. So far as our own affairs are concerned, 'SO far as the actions of the members of the Government are concerned, these stand upon a different basis, and as to these I shall be prompt to accept any challenge that my right hon. friend or any of his followers may see fit to make in this House.

My right hon. friend has no intention of allowing any investigation. He does not appreciate the position from which this matter has been approached by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House; or, if he does appreciate it, he will not accede to our request for an investigation. We are not making charges against the members of the Government; we do not say that members of the Government made a million or two or ten million dollars out of the operations of the Shell Committee. No one makes such a charge, and no one says that any member of the Shell Committee stole anything, although I will try, before I get through, to show that they made pretty big profits. I have no criminal charge to prefer against the members of the Shell Committee; but I suppose that unless I can go that far my right hon. friend will tell me that I have not complied with his requirements, and so cannot have an investigation. We stand on our sovereign rights as representing the people and demand an investigation of the expenditure of our money.

What is wrong with my hon. friend?
Name a dollar of Canadian money that has been spent. [DOT]

My hon. friend has not been here lately, and I suppose he is trying to make up for lost time. Those of us who have been here and attending to our parliamentary duties can take this discussion in a quiet, businesslike way. But I will show my hon. friend a good many Canadian dollars spent before I am through

-I'll try to anyway. My hon. friend probably was not here when, early in the session, the Minister of Finance admitted, in reply to a question by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that we were paying our full proportion of the cost of this war. We are going to pay for supplying the Canadian troops with ammunition, just as we pay for supplying them with clothes. - The Finance Minister has stated on more than one occasion that we are paying for these supplies out of the moneys raised in Canada by the internal loan. At the end of the war there will be an accounting with the Imperial Government and whatever proportion is ours to pay will have been paid already, and whatever proportion is not ours will come back from the British Government. Therefore, Sir, we are spending our own money. We have now, in all probability, about one twenty-fifth of the British troops at the front; before the war closes we may have one-fifteenth- and I hope we shall. We have in Canada three hundred munition factories, according to all the evidence, and we are told that there are three . thousand such factories in Great Britain. On that basis, we have one-tenth the productive power in munitions that they have, but probably our factories are not so great as theirs. At any rate, we haye a fairly large proportion of the burden of supplying munitions-and that is what we are talking about, the purchase by this old Shell Committee in Canada of munitions for the use of the British and Canadian troops. That being so, we are spending our own money, and this Opposition is only asking that which is the right of any Opposition, or of any representatives of the people, to investigate how our money has been expended. When Parliament meets every year a resolution is passed in the House without quibble-it goes through as a mere matter of form-referring to the Public Accounts Committee the 'accounts of the previous fiscal year. Do we have to lay a charge against any official to have access to these accounts? No, they come to us as a matter of right. All we are asking here is that you give us the right to investigate these munitions accounts. And I submit that the Prime Minister is dodging behind a most unreasonable barrier when he says: You cannot get an investigation, you cannot investigate the expenditure of your own money to the extent of perhaps two or three hundred million dollars, until you lay a charge against some one. His followers may

consider that they are loyal to him when they applaud him in taking a stand like thait. But let them go to their constituencies and see what even their own supporters will tell them about that. There is nothing to which the people of Canada are giving so muich attention, outside the prosecution of the war, as the question whether the Prime Minister is going to give the people a chance to get to the bottom of this unsavory mess.
I addressed this House something over a month ago and went into certain phases of this matter rather exhaustively.	I will try, in my brief remarks to-night not to repeat anything I said on that occasion. It may be impossible entirely to keep away from it all. The Prime Minister waxed eloquent over the question of patronage, and wants the people of Canada to believe that there has been no party patronage in the handling of affairs by this old Shell Committee. No wonder my hon. friends opposite smile when that proposition comes before them, for they know a little better than we do just what they have done and how far they have succeeded. The Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) says there has been no patronage. I gave a few illustrations of the forming of mushroom company after mushroom company. I named about fifteen of these concerns, including some that had been formed by Conservative heelers and workers, to manufacture shells and rake in some easy money. Take the case I pointed to in New Glasgow, N.S., where the local Conservative committee organized two shell companies. Take the case of the company that sent in 500 shells which were rejected, and afterwards sent them back again-I will not go over that sordid story again. It may be possible that the lives of our men, and not only their lives but the result of a battle may turn on the use of those rejected shells. Yet, though the Prime Minister had knowledge of these facts for the last four or five months, these same people have been allowed to go on and manufacture shells. And yet these hon. gentlemen tell us that there is no patronage. Wherever you go throughout Canada you will find the same condition of affairs. But I discussed that on a former occasion, as I have said, and shall not devote further time to it.
The Prime Minister asks what would happen if we went into an investigation. Well, I can tell him a few things that would happen. He would find that this
Shell Committee, instead of buying shells of all kinds in Canada cheaper than they were bought in England, paid in most cases at least 25 per cent more than was being paid for shells of the same kind at the same time in England. I will prove this statement before I am through. And I will not do it by bringing forward documents that I am afraid to read.

Who is afraid to read
documents?
The Minister of Publi'c Works (Mr. Rogers) was not here, and does not know to what I refer.
The Prime Minister did not say-

He did not read them.
And I say it is pretty small business of the Prime Minister to bring a document before this House and say: The gentleman who sent this document-Mr. Lloyd George in this case-says he does not think I should read the prices. And then he starts in to read the rest of the document, and when we object to that merely gives certain deductions. I have seen a few pretty sharp tricks in this House but this comes the nearest to that kind of thing that I have ever known to be practised by a prime minister. If he wants to be fair to the House he will lay that document on the Table, and then we can make our own deductions. I have some information on this subject, and I am going to take all the time that is necessary to support the deductions I have made; and I think before I am through I shall have convinced the Minister of Militia anyhow that he had better have that document laid on the Table that we may make our own comparisons and draw our own inferences. I want to tell the Minister of Militia, and the Prime Minister also, that if they will lay that document on the Table they won't he able to substantiate the deductions which the Prime Minister has drawn from it and given to this House.
I state as a fact and I am prepared to prove, I will prove to-night by evidence that I think will satisfy even my hon. friends opposite, and I will prove to the country beyond the possibility of dispute, if my hon. friends will give us a committee, that the prices in Canada are not lower but are higher than they are in Britain and higher than they are in the United States. I will prove that from the lips of the Minister of Militia himself, and from the documents out of his department.

*The next reason put forward by the right hon. Prime Minister for not appointing this committee was that the British Government had not demanded it; the British Government say: "We are not asking for a committee." No, of course they are not'. But do my hon. friends realize that this Empire is at war? I do not think they do. I listened to the Prime Minister this afternoon for over two hours, and, apart from a slurring remark which he made to my right hon. leader at the beginning of his speech, he entirely forgot the fact that the Empire needed munitions. According to his argument, the prime object of the Shell Committee was to distribute patronage and distribute business over Canada regardless of whether we got shells this year or next year, or any year, so long as we got the money distributed among the Canadian people. I should like my hon. friends to point out any other argument or reason put forward by the Prime Minister for obtaining this business and carrying it on. It makes no difference to the Prime Minister whether the British Empire is supplied with munitions or not.

What is wrong over there anyhow? A gentleman who has been in Parliament as long as the gentleman who has just said "rot" had better stand up when saying it.
I will stand up, and I will say you are talking rot.
I am glad you stand up. No, Mr. Speaker, do not call him to order. He is the last man in the world I would call to order.
It is my duty to call the hon. member for North Essex to order, and to ask him to withdraw the expression he has just used.
I will gladly withdraw the remark, but if I was talking as the hon. gentleman is, I am sure that I would believe that I was talking rot.	.

It is immaterial to me, because if there is a man whom I would not try to answer, or with whom I would, not enter into an altercation, it is the hon. member for North Essex. So he is at liberty to talk any way he likes, so far as I am concerned.
I do not talk very often.
Order.

The Prime Minister took a great deal of credit to the Government over the fact that they had been able to distribute, or rather had been able to receive, orders for $380,000,000 worth of munitions in Canada, and expected to have orders for $500,000,000 before the close of the war. He took a great deal of credit to the Government because the manufacturing establishments of Canada had been kept busy. For about an hour of his time he attempted to show that we on this side of the House were casting slurs and insinuations, and I think I could go so far as to say that we were saying disrespectful things of the manufacturers of Canada. Who has heard any member on this side of the House finding fault witih the manufacturers of Canada over the manufacture of shells? No man has- ever hear4 me find fault with them, and I have addressed the House at considerable length on this question; nor has any other Ihon. member on this side of the House found fault with them. In fact, I went so far as to say that we wanted munitions and I did not care who made them. I even said that if the Prime Minister were the owner of the only industry in Canad,a that could make munitions and make them quickly the order should be given to the Prime Minister. I say that here to-night. We do not care who gets the orders; what we do care about . is to have the business so done that we will get the munitions and get them in time and at reasonable prices. That is all we have to say about it; and our complaint about the Shell Committee is that they did not get the munitions in time and did not get them at a reasonable price.
My right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) made the statement this afternoon that - at a certain time not more than two per cent of the shells had been delivered. He did, not say that only two per cent had been delivered at the present time but that at the time of which he was speaking, that was last July, only 2 per cent had been delivered. We knew that more than that had been delivered at the present time. In fact, I can tell my friends almost to a shell how many shells have been delivered, and I can inform the House that there has been delivered about one-third of the shrapnel, a little less than that of the 18-pounder high-explosive shell's, -and around one-third

of the 18-pounders; a good deal less than that of the 4.5's. When you come to the larger shells, prac'ticaly none have been delivered. What we complain of is that the Shell Committee, instead of organizing the industries of Canada for the purpose of turning out a shell that was some good, made it their principal object in life to get business for themselves and their own companies. I complain that in order to keep up the prices for themselves and their own companies they were compelled to allow every other person manufacturing in Canada to get a bigger price than the justice of the case demanded or would allow under the conditions. That is my charge-I should not call it a charge but that is the fault I find with the old Shell Committee, and that is the reason why I want this matter investigated. I want to show how this business has been carried on, and I want to show the people of this country how their money and not British money has been squandered-because I cannot use any milder term-by the Shell Committee, squandered, not 'by the thousands or hundreds of thousands, but' by the million, in taking big contracts to themselves and then, in order to get these big contracts themselves, they were compelled to give contracts to many other people at the same exorbitant prices. I think I will come pretty near proving, before I am through, that I listened in vain to my right hon. friend for any reason other than the one I have given as to why this committee of investigation should not be granted. I am going to give the right hon. gentleman some further reasons, and I hope that I will convince him that he had not 'all the information under his hand, and that he will admit when I have finished that further light has been vouchsafed to him, sufficient to make him change his mind 'and admit that the people of Canada, in their sovereign right, have the right to demand an investigation of the expenditure of their money. That is what we are asking for. If there is gross suspicion cast around the expenditure of that money, then I think we have the right to come here and demand that the Prime Minister give us the right to investigate these matters, but not by a Royal Commission. The Parliament of Canada is not running this country by Royal Commissions; it ought not to be anyway. But, Sir, we have the right to ask an investigatioon by a committee of this House, representing the
people of Canada, who have the legal right to investigate these matters and pronounce upon them. We have had one illustration of the workings of Royal Commissions. I bad occasion to point out something of the way in which this Royal Commission conducted its affairs about six weeks ago, and I am happy to say I think that did them good. I do not think they would have got the evidence of this Mr. Stone, from New York, taken on a Sunday in the Chateau Laurier if it had not been for some things that had been said in this House. I think that did this Royal Commission a great deal of good. But, after all, that Royal Commission did not even get on the fringe of the subject. They never touched the fuses at all, the most nefarious transaction in the whole sordid story. My hon. friend shakes his head? I repeat it-the most nefarious transaction in the whole sordid story. With the fate of the Empire trembling in the balance, with uncertainty as to whether it is going to be victory or failure, and, a,s my right hon. leader pointed out, with the Allied troops pressing the Germans at the battle of the Marne and having to stop because they had not ammunition, for one long year they were in that position, fighting against horrible odds, without the munitions with which to fight, while the Shell Committee was grinding out shrapnel shells by the millions; yes, by the five, six, and seven millions, grinding out high-explosive shells by the million, grinding out 4-.5 shells by the million, and making no attempt whatever to get fuses. A high-explosive shell of any kind, without a fuse, is just about as efficacious against the enemy as if you went up to Parliament Hill and got a lot of those old round iron balls which they used a hundred years ago, and fired them. Without a fuse you cannot explode a shell, and without the explosion it practically accomplishes nothing. And yet, they dilly-dallied and fooled away the time, what for?; in order that my hon. friend's friend, Colonel Allison, of New York, might be able to make his arrangements, get his combinations together, his sub-contractors together, and arrange for his rake-off; in order that Colonel Allison, the only honest man, according to the evidence of the Minister of Militia and Defence, might be able, I repeat, to get together his combinations, to get together his sub-contractors, to arrange where the contracts were to go, to arrange thn sub -

contracts by which the shells were to be manufactured, and in order to provide for his share of the profits of the transaction in the end. And this Empire on the brink of destruction because we had not fuses with which to explode the shells that were manufactured.
These are some of the things which I charge against this Shell Committee, a committee which existed almost a year, a committee of experts, with a gentleman so expert as the lion. Minister of Militia at their head, which frittered away ten months and made no attempt whatever to get fuses; a committee which devoted its energies to machining shrapnel and high-explosive shells because it could make one hundred, two hundred, and three hundred per cent on the transaction; a -committee which forgot all about the objects for which it was appointed, which forgot the real necessities of the case; and you tell me that we are unpatriotic, that we have no right to come here and ask for an investigation into that condition of affairs. I tell you that it is insulting the intelligence of Parliament, it is insulting the intelligence of the public of Canada, for the Prime Minister and his back-bench followers to make the statement that we are not entitled to an investigation under these conditions.
My hon. friend the Minister of Militia went into a somewhat lengthy description of the constitution of the Shell Committee, and I desire to read from Hansard, pages 296-297, for I think it is necessary, in order to make my argument complete, that I should give in detail the contract which resulted in the formation of the Shell Committee. I am glad I have set my hon. friends thinking over there; it is a good sign when they get on the anxious seat, and I am very glad that they are now giving me some attention.
I must apologize. I do not know one word my hon. friend said, hut if he has anything to say concerning me I wish he would repeat it.

I have so much to say that it is not necessary to repeat it. My hon. friend will he satisfied by the time I get through. The minister says that on 24th August he received a cablegram from the War Office as follows:
Can you provide or obtain from American trade shell empty shrapnel, Q.F. guns, 18-pr., without cases or fuses. If so, what rate delivery could you promise?

That meant an ordinary empty 18-pounder shrapnel shell. If any one wants a description of an ordinary 18-pounder empty shell, the minister gave it to us; he will find it on page 295 of Hansard. He gave a pretty nearly accurate description of an empty shrapnel shell and I am going to read it. You remember, Mr. Speaker, that the minister had on his desk, not only a shell but a cartridge. I have forgotten whether he had the fuse on the end of the shell or not; I think not. This is his description:
This is what we term an empty shell (showing the whole shell). This is the steel shell case (showing), with the copper driving band on it fitting into the grooves of the barrel. The brass part which fits on the top of the shell case is called the fuse-plug, and in the shell at the present time is a powder cup empty.
and so on. . That was how the minister described the empty shell. The British Government wanted to know if they could obtain a price from the American trade. There was an answer stating that they could get large quantities from their neighbours. On August 26, the War Office cabled the Militia Department again as follows:
Tour telegram August 26. Please cable quo- tation 100,000 segment shells, Q.F. guns, 18-pr. shells only. Presume you have detailed drawings and specifications. Can you arrange inspection. Am sending specifications of 15-pr. shrapnel shells, quotation required 100,000 of these.
'There was another communication on the 2nd September, but it is not important, because it does not form part of the contract, and I am only reading those portions of the correspondence which allude to the contract. On September 2, the minister wired the War Office as follows:
Have organized committee of manufacturers on shells. They guarantee 20,000 by first November and 300,000 monthly thereafter. May be able to largely increase this amount.
On the 11th of September another cablegram was sent to the War Office, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the members of this House will pay attention to this particular communication, because, to my mind, it is one of the most remarkable cablegrams in the whole correspondence: (Reads):
Regarding shells. Have discovered one firm, Canadian General Electric, which guarantees alone to manufacture by the first of January 100,000, either 18-pr. or 15pr., and 100,000 monthly thereafter. Important to know will you want more than the 200,000 already placed.
As early as the 11th of September, we had a firm of the standing, ability, and reputation of the Canadian General Electric

Company, stating that they could manufacture 100,000 shells by the 1st day of January, and 100,000 monthly after that.
What year was that:

In 1914, right after the commencement of the war. So far as my information goes, the Canadian 'General Electric Company did not get an order until they lay down in the summe; of 1915, and then it was for only 25,000 18-pounder high-explosive shells. That cablegram, I think is one of the most remarkable parts of the whole correspondence. If there is a manufacturing concern in Canada with which I am intimately acquainted, it is the Canadian. General Electric Company. I have done business with them for the last 12 years; I know that they are able to manufacture anything that any other firm in Canada can manufacture; they have the money, the organization, the ability, and the plant, and I know that, if they had been given an opportunity, they would have manufactured the shells, as they are doing now.
