What does the machining of shrapnel shells consist of anyway? . A shrapnel shell consists of what is called a blank. In the first place it is a lump of steel; it is then put through a big machine, which punches a hole in it, and it then comes out and is known as a forging; it is then pointed at the nose; the walls are Straight and are about eight or nine inches long; it is then put in a lathe, and is turned to the exact size, inside and out. You would think that a turning lathe was a new invention in the commercial history of the world, from the way these men talk-that it had not been seen in Canada before. I admit that in order to do this work economically the manufacturers had to get a different kind of turning lathe from the one ordinarily used in a machine shop. But there is not a little foundry in any small town in Canada that was not anxious to go into this business, anxious to invest $15,000 or $20,000 in additional plant in order to get a contract. I know of one plant in New Brunswick, not manufacturing 18-pounders, but 4-5, which is an altogether bigger proposition. They have an order, I think, for 40,000 rounds of 4-5, and it only cost them $12,000 to instal the necessary plant. Gentlemen opposite tell us these fanciful stories about the enormous expense in buying the necessary machinery and carrying on this business, but I am happy to	say that even	if they
can fool some of the people they cannot fool all of us. As I was saying, the shell is put in a lathe and turned to the exact size; and,, Mr. Speaker, you would think that the turning of a piece of metal to a certain size to fit a certain gauge, or caliper as it is called, was some mechanical art wlhich should be rewarded by means of a statue and a medax. Why, there is not a little foundry in the country to-day that is not turning every
day of its life shafts and bearings, and they are turning these to the one-thousandth part of an inch, doing the work so fine that nothing else has to be done to the metal. And yet gentlemen opposite tell us that these men, who have been doing such delicate work as this for hundreds of years cannot turn a shrapnel shell down to a certain gauge.
Exactly the same process is followed with regard to the inside of the slhell. It is turned on the inside until the hole is just big enough, and then a seat is threaded in which to insert a brass socket. The brass socket is threaded on the inside and outside, and on the inside of the brass socket you have simply a plug, which is taken away when the shell is filled, and a fuse put in its place. That is all there is to machining an 18-pounder shell. The work in connection with the machining of an 18-pounder high explosive i.s even less than that, because the high explosive simply consists of a bar 3 inches in diameter and 15 or 20 feet long. The bar is sawed to the proper length, and is then put in a lathe and turned to the proper size. Then a little hole is bored in the base of the shell. The idea is that as the propelling or firing charge is beibind, and as the shell itself is filled with a high explosive or gun-cotton, in case there was a pin hole or sand hole through the . base of the shell, the explosive inside the shell might explode before it left the gun and there would be trouble. So in order to make assurance doubly sure, they bore out a little place in the base of the shell about 2 inches across and f inches deep, and insert in that a piece of forged steel which is threaded on the outside. This is done in order to make sure that the shell will not explode before it leaves the gun. That is all there it to machining an 18-pounder high-explosive. They do not even have to insert a brass socket in the nose of it, A hole is drilled through the centre and a plug put into that, and when they want to load the shell they take out the plug and put in the fuse. These are the operations in which such great mechanical ingenuity has been displayed by the manufacturers of Canada!

the difference between success and defeat in the titanic struggle through which we are passing.	.

I find that they get an order for 1,000,000 clips for 18-pounders. Let me describe what a clip is. When the breech block is thrown open on the 18-pounder it is supposed automatically to eject the empty case just as in the case of the ordinary rifle. When you throw the breach block open the empty case is ejected. But if the case is not automatically ejected they provide each gun with what is called a clip. This consists simply of two pieces of metal f inches wide, 14 or 16 gauge thickness, and a little more than 3 inches in length. These two pieces of metal are crossed over one on the other at right angles, the ends are bent in to catch the rim of the cartridge and then if the cartridge does not come out with the opening of the breechblock, they catch the end of it with the clip and pull it out. These clips are made sometimes of brass and sometimes of steel and they are fastened to-

gether in the centre. I do not know whether 20 cents is a reasonable price for these little clips or not. I make no charges as to whether it is right or wrong, I only want to have the white light thrown upon this transaction, and if it is all right, why, it is all right because I am finding no fault. I must, however, have a few words with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia before I sit down as to the question of prices and I therefore think that I will have to leave some of this material. I have pointed out that the members of this Shell Committee were taking contracts at $5.70 each for machining an enormous quantity of 18-pounder high explosives ; they were taking contracts to themselves at $5.15 for machining enormous quantities of 18-pounder shrapnel shells and they were taking contracts to themselves at $6.70 for machining enormous quantities of 4:5-inch Howitzer shells. I do not have to argue with any hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to get them to understand that when they were giving contracts to themselves at these big prices they had to give contracts to the other 300 men who were doing business with the committee. That is the trouble. Of course, I do not mean to say that there were actually 300 men making shells. There were not more than 100 other people making shells altogether. But they were taking to themselves these enormous orders at big prices and they were compelled to give the same big prices to the other people. I have given the information to the House, and I can almost give it the weight of evidence, that when Mr. Jones, of the Canada Cement Company, wanted to cut down the prices of these goods they would not allow him to do it on the plea that he could not do the work for the price that he said he could do it for. It must be in the mind of every hon. gentleman opposite that the real reason was that if they gave contracts to Mr. Jones at a lower price they would be compelled to take these contracts themselves at no higher prices.
I have another bit of information which I can prove if the Government will give me a committee. In the month of August, or September-I do not know which hut I think it was in September-a gentleman whose name I can furnish at the proper time, went to Mr. Thomas, the representative of Mr. Lloyd George in the city of Ottawa and told him that he wias going to submit a tender for machining shells- I am not sure whether it was 18-pounder high explosive or	shrapnel-at $1.40
apiece. A few days after that he saw in the office of the Shell Committee, a tender to do this work at $1.40. Mr. Thomas was called away to Montreal and was gone for three or four days. He supposed that, as a matter of 'course, the contract would be

I think I appreciate some of the rights and duties of a member of Parliament. You may call me a Radical or anything else you like, but I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen opposite,, if I have ever made a statement in this House that I was unable to back up and prove to the hilt. I have a word with my hon. friend the Minister of Militia about prices. I want to take him back to his famous speech of January 26, 1916, in this House. Early in my remarks I explained, how the contract for the first 200,000 shells was made. The minister says that the price arrived at was $8.55. I am not positive whether that was for the shrapnel or high explosive.
It was all shrapnel.

It was 18-pounder shrapnel. My hon. friend said in his speech on January 26:	.
The price of $8.55 was arrived at by the experts of the Militia Department, who made their calculations with the assistance of machinists and large steel manufacturers throughout the country.
The Prime Minister was compelled to admit this afternoon that the price for the Canadian shrapnel was somewhat higher in Canada than in England. Now I want to show my hon. friend the 'Minister of Militia what information he had in his department about the price of empty shrapnel shells. And

in order that there may be no misunderstanding about what an empty shell is I will describe it, and if I am wrong the minister can set me right. As I understand it, an empty shrapnel shell consists of a blank piece of steel; and at the beginning the Nova, Scotia Steel Company got an order for 300,000 of these blanks at 45 cents each. I do not think this price was paid for the blank's later on, but it was in the beginning. Then there is a forging; the forging of that shell cost $1.25 each. I think it is really $1.30, but the price came down after the first order. Then there is the machining and assembling at $5.55, which I have already explained. Then'there is a brass socket. I have not one here, but I can illustrate it with this tumbler. The shell is rimmed out perhaps 2J inches in diameter, and there is a piece of metal which is threaded on the outside and turns into the top of the shell. This is also threaded on the inside, in which, we find the fuse when the shell is loaded and ready for action. I do not know whether the price paid for these brass sockets was a fair price or not, but I do know from a rather lengthy and somewhat inquisitive investigation that the price which the committee paid for brass sockets was 40 cents. A brass socket, to start with, is a piece of brass about 21 inches in diameter and about 11 inches deep; this is turned and threaded on the outside, bored <out, and then threaded on the inside. 'Whether that is worth 40 cents I do not know. I should like to have a chance of investigating it, but it seems to me that a man would not have to make more than three or four million of them at that price in order to make enough money to keep him going for the summer. Next comes the plug. At the beginning of the war this was made of brass. It is a piece of metal which fits on the inside of the brass socket before the shell has been fused. When you insert the fuse, the plug is taken out and thrown away. The price of the plug was 25 cents. Later on they got the price down to 10 cents by using galvanized iron instead of brass, and I think in some cases they are now using wood. At any rate, at the present time galvanized iron is being used in large quantities at 10 cents, and I have heard that the Munitions Board has cut the price down lower than that. But that is only hearsay, and I am only making statements to-night that I can prove up to the hilt if 1 am given an opportunity of doing so, and I am making them on my responsibility as a member of this House.

I have really just covered one or two phases, and I want to take up some other matters.
I certainly do not object, but I would dearly love to get a clip at the hon. gentleman.

You could get it on
Thursday.
iSir ROBERT BORDEN: I think the minister, upon reflection, has come to the conclusion [DOT] that there is not yery much to

answer, and therefore he will consent to adjourn the debate.
I move the adjournment of the debate.

Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN moved the adjournment of the House. He said: I intended that we should go on with this debate on Thursday, but I understand that some arrangement has been made between the whips on account of which some hon. gentlemen may not be here on Thursday. Therefore I am willing to adjourn the debate until Tuesday, and take up estimates on Thursday and Friday if that will more generally meet the convenience of hon. gentlemen. If we go into estimates, we will take up Labour, Justice and Railways.
If Railways will suit my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham).

If an arrangement has
been made, of course we will conform to it, although I understood we were going on on Thursday, with this debate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So did I.
However, if the proposal suits the convenience of hon. members we will acquiesce in it.

I suppose I ought not tQ ask too many favours, but on account of some personal matters that have cropped up by cable to-day, I think it will be difficult for me to be here the first of next week.
I should prefer Thursday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then we will have the continuation of the speech of my hon. friend on Thursday, one speech in reply, and then adjourn the debate and go into Estimates for the rest of Thursday and the whole of Friday.
Railway Estimates will suit me on Thursday, but I am not so sure about Friday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then we will not take them up on Friday, hut on Thursday, if at all.

Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.38 p.m.
Thursday, March 9, 1916.
